arXiv:2611.22456v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: Omnimodal large language models (Omni-LLMs) integrate audio, video, and text for multimodal reasoning, yet remain vulnerable to cross-modal hallucinations, where one modality improperly influences predictions about another. Existing training-free decoding methods mitigate these errors through modality perturbation or relevance-based weighting. However, due to interference from irrelevant modality cues during fusion and difficulty detecting shared errors, these methods may suppress correct unimodal predictions and allow erroneous consensus to persist. To address these limitations, we propose Provenance-Aware Consensus Decoding (PACD), a training-free framework for mitigating cross-modal hallucinations. PACD comprises two complementary paths based on whether the branches reach consensus. For non-consensus cases, Relevance-Guided Candidate Arbitration identifies task-relevant unimodal evidence and selectively arbitrates between predictions using alternative candidates. For consensus cases, Provenance-Based Consensus Recovery leverages the outranking principle to evaluate the consistency and strength of layer-wise modality evidence for alternative answers, selectively resolving erroneous consensus under confidence constraints. Extensive experiments on four Omni-LLMs and five benchmarks across two tasks demonstrate the superiority of PACD. Compared to existing methods, PACD achieves up to 27.6% relative improvement over standard decoding across CMM, AVHBench, and SVHalluc for cross-modal hallucination mitigation, and an average relative improvement of 7.7% over best baseline across OmniVideoBench and FutureOmni for general audio-visual reasoning.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon Route 53 Domains now lets you restore an expired or recently deleted domain yourself, using the Amazon Route 53 console, AWS CLI, or AWS SDKs.
  • To restore a domain, you enter the domain name, review the restoration price, accept the charge, and submit the request.
  • According to recent reports, to learn more, see Restoring an expired or deleted domain in the Route 53 Developer Guide, or visit the Amazon Route 53 Domains page.

Amazon Route 53 Domains now lets you restore an expired or recently deleted domain yourself, using the Amazon Route 53 console, AWS CLI, or AWS SDKs. Previously, restoring a domain required a request to AWS Support. Now you can recover a domain lost to a missed renewal, an expired payment method, or an accidental deletion, and restore the website, email, and applications that depend on it.

To restore a domain, you enter the domain name, review the restoration price, accept the charge, and submit the request. Route 53 works with the top-level domain (TLD) registry to reactivate the registration and return the domain to your AWS account. Most TLD registries support restoration, and each registry sets how long after expiration or deletion a domain can still be restored. Restoring a domain typically costs more than registering or renewing one.

According to recent reports, to learn more, see Restoring an expired or deleted domain in the Route 53 Developer Guide, or visit the Amazon Route 53 Domains page. For a complete list of supported TLDs, see the Route 53 TLD list. For pricing, visit the Route 53 pricing page.

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.22432v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fast System-1 models enable responsive actions but struggle with complex or unfamiliar tasks. Large language model (LLM)-based System-2 provides strong reasoning capabilities, yet repeated invocation incurs substantial latency and computational costs. To bridge this gap, we propose JevRSI, a System-1/System-2 collaboration framework that transforms LLM reasoning into transferable decision support through recursive harness improvement. A Jev-style System-1 model enables low-latency action selection, while an asynchronous System-2 LLM develops a modular harness. The harness integrates procedures, state memory, and world models to provide decision contexts spanning the past, present, and future. Utility-driven retrieval selects modules based on both contextual relevance and their utility on previous tasks. Environmental feedback guides targeted revisions and enables recursive self-improvement. Experiments across three datasets show that JevRSI consistently improves decision quality, matching or surpassing LLM agents in several settings. It preserves low-latency execution with favorable performance-cost trade-offs. Moreover, System-2 development interventions decrease as the harness evolves, amortizing System-2 costs through continuous improvement. Our project is available at https://github.com/usail-hkust/JevRSI.

Latest Update: Give Your Coding Agents a Memory You Own

📅 03 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1577 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I work across several machines, and I switch coding agents depending on the task.
  • Earlier this year, Software Forgets: Agent Traces Are the Memory made the case that coding agents already produce the record we keep losing.
  • Sources indicate that while the diagnosis is correct, traces are only potential memory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I work across several machines, and I switch coding agents depending on the task. Every one of them meets my projects as a stranger. The reasoning from “last Tuesday” disappears when the session ends. Each new agent, on each new host, starts from zero.

Earlier this year, Software Forgets: Agent Traces Are the Memory made the case that coding agents already produce the record we keep losing. As they search a codebase, try approaches, hit errors, read documentation, and change direction, they leave behind a dense account of not just what changed, but why.

Sources indicate that while the diagnosis is correct, traces are only potential memory. The session logs of an agent are still just an archive. You cannot grep your way to “why did we move off the streaming parser?” across ten thousand turns. For an agent to use those traces while it works, they need indexing, retrieval, ranking, and exact provenance.

That is what funes provides. It is a durable memory layer for your agents (Claude Code, Codex, pi, and Hermes). It is built from the sessions already on your machine. It works locally and becomes part of your agent's normal workflow with one command. When you want it to, it can also travel to a Hugging Face dataset you own, private by default.

It has been revealed that funes is a single binary. Its default inference backend has no ML runtime dependency, and embedding and reranking happen on your machine. Install it:.

That one add command builds the first index, gives the agent recall and get tools, and installs the automation that indexes each completed turn. Indexing is incremental, with fresh runs adding new turns rather than embedding the whole history again. The older and deeper content can backfill in bounded steps.

From there, you just work. When a task touches a past decision, rationale, or finding, the agent can reach for recall itself. You do not need to remember the old session or paste its context into the newly introduced one.

With funes added, recall happens inside the conversation. The agent reaches for its memory on its own and names the session behind its answer.

Industry observers note that recall returns the original text, not a summary, and reveals exactly where it came from (the agent, timestamp, session, and turn). Each result includes a get command that opens the full turn and its surrounding context.

Sources indicate that underneath, one deterministic pipeline parses every supported trace into the same turn-and-block shape, chunks it, embeds it with a pinned local model, and writes it to a local Lance dataset. A query combines vector and BM25 search, fuses their rankings, reranks the candidates with a cross-encoder, reweights them by recency, and attaches neighboring chunks.

That design gives funes three important properties:.

Recent findings suggest that the agent as a stranger problem is already solved on one machine. But memory gets more useful when the next agent is running somewhere else.

To make a memory follow your work, bind one when you add funes to an agent:.

Sources indicate that the bind publishes your current memory there. funes then keeps it current, indexing each turn locally and publishing at session boundaries. The agent recalls from it throughout. Run the same command on another machine and the memory follows you there.

Underneath, the local memory is a Lance dataset, and the shared memory is a Hugging Face dataset (private by default) you own.

It has been revealed that before anything reaches the Hub, credentials have already been redacted during indexing. Publishing then scans every chunk again and withholds anything that still looks like a secret. The scanner behind this is documented in SECURITY.md, including what it does and doesn't cover.

Industry observers note that when an agent reads a remote memory, funes caches the dataset files locally, so warm queries return to local speed. The Hub supplies the ownership, access control, versioning, and distribution it already supplies for other datasets. Your memory does not become an account in a separate memory service, and you do not rent it back through an API.

Recent findings suggest that recall is shaped for agents. When you want to put a question to a memory yourself, use ask. It reads your local memory by default:.

It has been revealed that or point it at a shared memory. We published a memory of funes development, so you can ask why funes works the way it does without creating a memory of your own:.

funes ask is the read-only, one-question sibling of funes add. It recalls the passages, hands them to a coding agent, and returns a grounded answer that names its sources. It does not install an integration or change the agent's persistent setup.

A retrieval miss is not papered over. If the passages do not support an answer, the agent says so. You can rephrase the question or add funes to the agent so it can search the memory iteratively during normal work.

Sources indicate that A shared memory is not tied to the agent or model that created it. Start a task in Claude Code, continue it in Codex next week, and the second agent can recall the first agent's reasoning. Use pi with a local model or one served through the Hugging Face router, then return to Claude.

Claude makes a decision; a hook indexes it; Codex recalls it in another session. The older hits in the demo are earlier recordings of the same experiment: an append-only memory remembered the rehearsals too.

This matters in a few different scopes:.

According to recent reports, published memories carry a dataset card and the funes tag, making them recognizable and discoverable on the Hub. The Hub already hosts open weights and datasets. funes adds open working memory. It holds the decisions, failed approaches, and rationale behind a project, queryable by another agent and traceable to the sessions that produced them.

A long investigation bloats a session until each turn costs more to carry the context than to do the work. The usual answers are to let the agent compact and carry on, or to write a handoff and start fresh. Recall is a third, so we measured them against each other on the handoff-vs-recall benchmark: two tasks whose answer cannot be reconstructed without the session prior knowledge.

Sources indicate that compaction is what most agents do by default, and it was the only one of the three whose result divided: it arrived on one task and never arrived on the other. Where it failed, its summary had flattened the findings that mattered. Recall returns the passages themselves, so a finding does not have to survive summarization.

Recall was the cheapest of the three on both tasks, 8x cheaper than a written handoff on one and 4x on the other.

The lighter segment of each bar is the one-time charge for preparing the channel, the handoff or the compaction, paid before the first question is asked and counted once. A cross marks a channel that never arrives, and so has no cost per success.

“To think is to forget differences, generalize, make abstractions.” — Jorge Luis Borges, Funes the Memorious.

Sources indicate that your agents already wrote the record. funes lives at github.com/huggingface/funes, one command away from turning that record into a memory the next agent can read, on whichever machine you happen to be on.

In a recent development, funes invents little of this. It leans on open-source embedding models good enough to run locally, on Lance's append-only datasets with cheap incremental writes, and on the Hub's caching and content-dedup for datasets. The work is in fitting them into a memory an agent can actually use.

Industry observers note that funes is open source too. Open an glitch for anything from an install snag to a recall that missed, or an agent you'd like supported.

Ran funes 1.3.0 on a machine with 19,195 coding-agent sessions already on disk (LongMemEval laid down in the real ~/.claude and ~/.codex layouts), 100 questions whose answer sits in exactly one session, scored by whether that session comes back. Disclosure: I maintain deja-vu, one of the tools in the same table.

Industry observers note that full index: 2h03m on an M4 pro laptop (308k chunks), 6.3s per query. With defaults: hit@1 9/100, hit@5 39, found@50 71. With --half-life 0: 19/46/71 — the 30-day recency half-life halves rank-1 on history older than a month, which is most of what's on a real disk; worth a mention in the docs. Once recency is off, the vector+rerank stack is clearly the best ranker in the table at rank five. The documented one-minute first pass leaves 218 of the 19k sessions indexed (0/100 answered), so the "about a minute" framing is really "about a minute until the embedding job starts".

Industry observers note that for comparison on the same corpus, deja-vu (plain BM25 over 24 agents' files) indexes in 29s and answers in 24ms at hit@1 18/100, hit@5 35. Corpus, drivers and every row: vshulcz.github.io/deja-vu/guide/day-zero.html - happy to be corrected if a setting I missed changes the numbers.

longmemeval does not really need semantic search: BM25 already gives the same ratio you mentioned IIRC, so for this use case this is pretty much expected that it is not worth paying the cost of evaluating the embeddings (this extra cost you see at indexing and recall time). funes shines when the information is actually difficult to find.

This capability gives administrators granular control over which types of data sources consumers can create, patch, or share, helping organizations enforce data governance requirements while enabling self-service analytics. Latest AI agent observability and governance across BigQuery and Looker

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1373 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that as enterprises move AI agents from experimental prototypes into production, data and platform teams are discovering that deploying an agent is only half the battle — you also need to see how it reasons, which data it touches, and what it costs to run.
  • Putting conversational and autonomous agents into production requires solving three operational challenges: tracing multi-step reasoning while protecting sensitive data, controlling token consumption and query spend, and evaluating answer accuracy before prompt or schema changes reach owners.
  • Running agents at scale means you need to see how they perform, what they cost, and what actions they take.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The front door to AI in the workplace.

It has been revealed that as enterprises move AI agents from experimental prototypes into production, data and platform teams are discovering that deploying an agent is only half the battle — you also need to see how it reasons, which data it touches, and what it costs to run. Today, we are announcing expanded AI agent observability and evaluation capabilities across Google Data Cloud, giving you unified visibility into your first-party (1P) data agents in BigQuery and Looker as well as custom third-party (3P) agents built with agent development frameworks such as Agent Development Kit (ADK) or LangGraph.

Putting conversational and autonomous agents into production requires solving three operational challenges: tracing multi-step reasoning while protecting sensitive data, controlling token consumption and query spend, and evaluating answer accuracy before prompt or schema changes reach owners. Let’s explore how our new agent observability and evaluation capabilities help you do this.

Running agents at scale means you need to see how they perform, what they cost, and what actions they take. We're rolling out a unified telemetry framework across Google's Agentic Data Cloud that works the same way for every agent: Capture telemetry from the agent, land it in BigQuery tables you own, and analyze it wherever your teams already work.

Unified agent observability framework capturing logging telemetry across 1P and 3P agents into BigQuery to surface performance and usage insights across developer and admin tools.

1. Capture telemetry from every first-party and custom agent.

First-party data agents: Out-of-the-box Conversational Analytics agents emit telemetry automatically with no setup required. Queries routed to BigQuery data agents in Gemini Enterprise through agent-to-agent (A2A) workflows (now GA) send Cloud Monitoring metrics, Cloud Trace spans, and BigQuery conversation logs straight into your agent's project.

Custom agents: Agents built with ADK or LangGraph stream the same structured telemetry into BigQuery through single-line SDK instrumentation.

Recent findings suggest that 2. Land telemetry in one governed home in BigQuery.

Conversation logging in BigQuery (GA): Managed 1P conversation logging writes to BigQuery tables you own, so you can inspect Conversational Analytics traces, including prompts and responses, directly in your data warehouse.

Governed by default: The Conversational Analytics API, now GA, includes always-on admin audit logs and optional data-read audit logs in Cloud Audit Logs, and supports VPC Service Controls, customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK), and regional and multi-regional data residency.

Sources indicate that 3. Analyze with dashboards wherever your teams work.

In BigQuery (GA): Agent monitoring provides prebuilt dashboards in BigQuery Studio to track usage, active sessions, top knowledge sources, and latency across BigQuery Conversational Analytics agents.

BigQuery Conversational Analytics dashboard in BigQuery Studio, giving admins visibility into usage, active sessions, top knowledge sources, and latency.

Looker Conversational Analytics dashboard in System Activity, giving admins visibility into usage, token consumption, and user feedback.

Custom Data Studio dashboard built on BigQuery Agent Analytics logs to track token consumption, latency, and user engagement.

Looker Block dashboard built on BigQuery Agent Analytics telemetry to monitor session volumes, tool execution latency, and token cost distribution.

Enterprise observability requires balancing diagnostic telemetry with strict data privacy boundaries. Because tracking features involve ingestion and storage costs, Google Data Cloud separates operational telemetry from conversation content so admins and agent owners can govern each layer independently.

At the project or organization level, admins can enable Cloud Monitoring (aggregate metrics such as request volume, latency, and token usage) and Cloud Trace (step-by-step spans for each request) across their environment, using Cloud Trace observability scopes to consolidate telemetry across multiple agent projects. To protect sensitive data, these operational metrics and sanitized first-party trace spans exclude customer core content (such as user prompts, model responses, internal thoughts, and generated SQL).

When you need deeper transcript auditing, agent owners and editors can opt in to conversation logging on a per-agent basis:.

Governed conversation logging in BigQuery: When enabled, a Google-managed service agent streams user prompts, responses, and turn-level telemetry into a customer-owned BigQuery table (agent_events) via the BigQuery Storage Write API, inheriting your dataset's IAM permissions, CMEK, and VPC Service Controls. Built-in privacy guardrails enforce a fail-closed check before each turn — skipping logging whenever a knowledge source uses row-level security, column-level policy tags, or dynamic data masking — while fail-open execution keeps your users' chat sessions uninterrupted if a logging error occurs.

Full trace trees for custom 3P agents: While 1P conversation logging intentionally strips low-level tool arguments and internal SQL, developers building custom agents on ADK or LangGraph can instrument their code with the open-source ADK plugin (BigQueryAgentAnalyticsPlugin). With a single-line setup, the SDK streams full tool-invocation execution trees, time-series telemetry, and multimodal payloads straight into BigQuery.

In-warehouse root cause and drift analysis: Because conversation logs land natively in your agent_events table, you don't need separate export pipelines to diagnose failures. You can run BigQuery AI functions (such as AI.GENERATE to summarize error patterns and AI.EMBED with VECTOR_SEARCH to cluster recurring problems) or use the open-source bigquery-agent-analytics Python SDK and Colab starter notebook for post-hoc semantic drift clustering and LLM-as-a-judge sentiment analysis.

As agent adoption grows, FinOps and platform teams need clear visibility into consumption alongside active controls to prevent runaway spend. With promotional trial pricing right now available for Conversational Analytics, now is a good time to establish baseline usage and cost guardrails:.

Granular token and latency tracking: In BigQuery conversation logs, each turn records input, output, thought, cached, and total token counts alongside total turn latency, while Looker System Activity reports estimated input and output tokens across your business intelligence (BI) workloads.

Turnkey observability dashboards: You can track projected token usage and engagement in the BigQuery Studio Monitoring tab and native Looker System Activity dashboards, or query agent_events log data via BigQuery SQL using the open-source seven-page Data Studio report template and self-hosted Streamlit app in the BigQuery Agent Analytics GitHub repository.

According to recent reports, active query and token spend caps: To prevent unexpected charges before they happen, you can configure per-query BigQuery byte scan caps (big_query_max_billed_bytes) on your agent, which use dry-run estimates to block oversized queries without incurring on-demand scan charges. For BigQuery and the Conversational Analytics API, you can also enforce daily input and output token quotas (in preview) per project, user, or agent in the Google Cloud console and gcloud CLI.

According to recent reports, runtime observability works alongside systematic evaluation. While logs and traces tell you how an agent behaved in production, evaluation benchmarks verify whether updates to your prompts, models, or data schemas improve SQL accuracy and answer quality before users experience a regression:.

Benchmarking with Prism: Our open-source evaluation tool, Prism, lets you test Conversational Analytics agents grounded in BigQuery tables or Looker Explores via the Conversational Analytics API using reusable test suites, regex assertions, and multi-region agent discovery (deployed behind an access layer such as Cloud IAP).

Unified evaluation and production analytics: Prism can stream completed evaluation runs directly into day-partitioned BigQuery tables in your project, placing your pre-deployment benchmark scores right alongside your production agent_events logs for side-by-side analysis in BigQuery and Looker.

Native BigQuery evaluations: First-party agent evaluations in BigQuery (built on the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform evaluation service with bring-your-own-service-account support) are available in preview via API and a guided Colab notebook.

Ready to bring visibility, governance, and cost control to your AI agents? Here is how to get started in three steps:.

Recent findings suggest that enable first-party agent observability. Turn on Cloud Monitoring and Cloud Trace in your project and opt in to per-agent conversation logging using the BigQuery agent monitoring guide, and track BI token consumption with the Looker Conversational Analytics overview and Looker System Activity documentation.

Instrument custom agents and deploy analytics dashboards. Add the BigQuery Agent Analytics SDK to your ADK or LangGraph agents, launch the open-source Data Studio report template or Streamlit app, and explore in-warehouse log analysis with the Colab starter notebook.

In a recent development, benchmark your agents and set cost guardrails. Run automated accuracy suites with Prism, and configure BigQuery byte scan caps and daily token quotas via Manage BigQuery costs for agents.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that this guide is a fully public, inexpensive recipe for making a small model substantially better at structured-output compliance.
  • In a recent development, structured output is one of the most common real-world tasks for LLMs, yet most benchmarks fold it into broader reasoning or extraction scores rather than measuring it on its own.
  • In a recent development, note that the training pipeline described here is not the one used to train the RL model described in the IFStruct blog.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that this guide is a fully public, inexpensive recipe for making a small model substantially better at structured-output compliance. We fine-tune LFM2.5-350M with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using the TRL library and evaluate it on the IFStruct benchmark. The full run takes around 500 samples and 100 training steps, small enough for a free-tier Colab or Kaggle GPU, and is available on GitHub. The results show that even a light fine-tuning procedure improves performance from 22.6% to 29.7% on the IFStruct benchmark.

In a recent development, structured output is one of the most common real-world tasks for LLMs, yet most benchmarks fold it into broader reasoning or extraction scores rather than measuring it on its own. Whether a model reliably returns valid, parseable output in the requested format and shape — schema compliance — is often what decides whether it can be wired into a downstream system at all.

In a recent development, note that the training pipeline described here is not the one used to train the RL model described in the IFStruct blog. This notebook doesn't aim to recreate the IFStruct benchmark score, but to show how task-specific fine-tuning of smaller models can improve performance and match that of far larger models.

This guide has two halves that run in different places:.

In a recent development, we will need uv for the Python tooling and llama.cpp for serving. Following the Liquid AI llama.cpp deployment docs, install llama.cpp with Homebrew and verify that llama-server is available:.

Before we begin, let's evaluate LFM2.5-350M on the IFStruct benchmark and see whether we can reproduce the reported score of 21.1%.

IFStruct is a benchmark for testing the validity of LLM outputs and schema adherence. The benchmark is open-source in Liquid4All/ifstruct, with the public benchmark dataset available on Hugging Face at LiquidAI/ifstruct-v1.0.

Recent findings suggest that for the eval comparison, we serve the model locally on the MacBook with llama.cpp. We will use the BF16 GGUF (LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M-GGUF).

Then we start the base-model server with the following command:.

Once the server is running, we can run the full benchmark with 2000 samples:.

Sources indicate that the IFStruct release blog reports 21.1% for LFM2.5-350M. Our local llama.cpp/BF16 setup measures 22.6%, close to the 21.1% reported in the IFStruct blog. We use this local result as the baseline for the same serving stack comparison.

Industry observers note that the full, runnable pipeline lives in the accompanying notebook. We will cover only the relevant pieces in this section.

According to recent reports, we use nvidia/Nemotron-RL-instruction_following-structured_outputs, which pairs each prompt with a target JSON Schema and an expected field count. We use about 500 samples for training.

Because the Nemotron data distribution differs from the IFStruct evaluation, we augment the prompts to close two gaps between them:.

We load LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M and attach a LoRA adapter. Because LFM2.5 uses a hybrid attention/convolution architecture, we target the LFM-specific module names:.

This trains ~6M parameters, about 1.66% of the model.

Then we define three reward functions, each on a [0, 1] scale, which score every completion on whether the extracted structure is correct:.

We combine the three as a weighted sum with reward_weights=[1.0, 0.5, 2.0].

We train for 100 steps with 8 generations per prompt group, sized for a free-tier 16 GB GPU:.

As you can see in the notebook, over the run, all three reward components climb, the KL from the reference model lifts off zero after warmup, and the truncated-completion fraction stays near zero.

Finally, we merge the LoRA adapter back into the base weights and save it as a single self-contained checkpoint, ready to convert to GGUF for serving:.

It has been revealed that after GRPO fine-tuning, we rerun the IFStruct evaluation. For this, we need to convert the merged model checkpoint into a BF16 GGUF. The converter script ships with the llama.cpp source, so we clone the repo once and install the converter's gguf package.

Then we serve the merged model with the following command:.

Then, we will run the full IFStruct evaluation again with the fine-tuned model:.

Comparing the two runs on the identical serving stack:.

The gains land exactly where the training aimed: the JSON pass rate rises by nearly 14 points (18.0% → 31.9%), while YAML stays mostly the same. While this is still below the Qwen3.5-2B score of 33.15%, it shows that even light task-specific fine-tuning can bring a small model close to a larger one.

A short GRPO run with about 500 samples and 100 steps can lift a small 350M parameter model from 22.6% to 29.7% on IFStruct. The takeaway is that a cheap, task-specific reward signal can make a small model substantially more reliable about form, closing much of the gap to models several times its size.

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.22407v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Robotic applications often rely on long-running operations, such as navigation, manipulation, and inspection, which in ROS~2 are commonly implemented as actions. Unlike topics and services, actions involve a structured lifecycle comprising goal submission and acceptance, feedback, status updates, result retrieval, and cancellation. Existing versions of ROSMonitoring support topics and services, but do not reconstruct this lifecycle or expose action-level events to a runtime-verification oracle. In this paper, we extend ROSMonitoring with runtime monitoring and enforcement for ROS~2 actions. Actions are declared directly in the monitoring configuration and automatically instrumented through the underlying ROS~2 communication endpoints. The generated monitor reconstructs action-level events, correlates them through goal identifiers, maintains the state of active goals, and translates violations into protocol-aware enforcement operations. These include goal rejection, cancellation, message suppression, and protocol-compliant responses generated directly by the monitor when the original communication cannot be forwarded. We evaluate the implementation through controlled stress tests that vary the number of action invocations, workload size, and clientâ€“server topology. The results show approximately linear growth in monitoring cost with repeated action invocations under a fixed workload, while larger action workloads and a greater number of configured clientâ€“server pairs introduce additional overhead. These results characterise the scaling behaviour of the current implementation under the tested sequential workloads while highlighting the main performance limitations of the current synchronous implementation.

#3447. Symbolic Abstraction Refinement

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (355 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Symbolic Abstraction Refinement

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (355 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.22404v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous systems choose actions whose outcomes are uncertain and are subject to time constraints. Probabilistic timed automata (PTAs) model exactly this, and verifying one answers a question about the system's decision-making: the maximum probability of reaching a goal, or the minimum probability of reaching a hazard, that a controller can guarantee. Verification normally works over symbolic states, each pairing a discrete location with a region of clock values, and its difficulty is that the best behavior generally varies within such a region. The PRISM verifier's most capable PTA method responds by splitting regions until each is uniform, rebuilding the transitions that reach them and propagating the split backward through the state graph of a stochastic game, a cascade of graph reconstruction that partitions regions the property never depends on. We present SYMAR, which instead makes the value function symbolic: each symbolic state carries a function from sub-regions of its clock region to probability bounds, so refinement is the appearance of new sub-regions in that function, and previously generated states are never split nor their incoming transitions reconstructed. Both sources of PTA nondeterminism, the timing and the choice of actions, are captured implicitly by the preimage computation that produces those sub-regions. Heuristic forward search then bounds how much refinement is done at all, expanding an And-Or graph from the initial state along the most promising behaviors so that effort is confined to the property-relevant fragment, guided by bounds and preferred actions from a single unrefined run of the existing method; a partial-refinement backup keeps the otherwise combinatorial sub-region count lean, and every stored interval provably contains the true probability. On the PRISM PTA benchmarks, whose subproblems recur in autonomous systems (distributed agreement under contention, leader election, and self-configuration without central coordination), SYMAR is up to 108x faster, solves an instance on which the existing method exhausts the time limit, and is markedly less sensitive to the deadline constant, resolving one instance in a 37-node search graph, unchanged as the deadline triples, where the existing method needs 86,380 abstract states and 73 refinement rounds.

Accelerated compliance with machine-readable evidence: Continuously monitor posture, record immutable exception justifications, run scheduled audits and export machine-readable audit evidence to help fast-track certification workflows.

Turn compliance and digital sovereignty into a business accelerator.

#3445. NeoMME: an efficient Multimodal-native and Multilingual Encoder

📅 03 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1549 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

NeoMME: an efficient Multimodal-native and Multilingual Encoder

📅 03 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1549 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that we introduce NeoMME, a family of 260M and 800M multilingual multimodal encoders.
  • We fine-tuned NeoMME for visual document retrieval using ColPali's page-image approach.
  • NeoMME is available in Hugging Face Transformers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that we introduce NeoMME, a family of 260M and 800M multilingual multimodal encoders. Unlike many generative visual language models, NeoMME does not use a separate pretrained vision tower or a causal language model. A single bidirectional Transformer processes both text tokens and raw image patches, and we train the entire model from scratch with a masked discrete-diffusion objective.

We fine-tuned NeoMME for visual document retrieval using ColPali's page-image approach. NeoMME-Retriever returns dense and late-interaction embeddings in one forward pass. Both model sizes lie on the ViDoRe v3 Pareto frontier for nDCG@10 and model size. At a matched 2048×2048 image input size on an NVIDIA L40S GPU, the 260M model encodes about 51 pages per second, or about twice ColModernVBERT's throughput. Hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization reduce late-interaction index storage from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page (255× smaller) while retaining more than 95% of baseline nDCG@10.

NeoMME is available in Hugging Face Transformers. We release all model checkpoints under the Apache 2.0 license.

According to recent reports, many recent visual document retrievers are adapted from pretrained generative visual language models. A separately pretrained vision encoder produces visual features, which a projector maps into the language model's input space. A causal decoder then processes the combined image and text representations. Retrieval, classification, and token labeling do not generate text autoregressively, so they do not require a causal decoder or the parameter and compute overhead of this architecture.

ModernBERT brought efficient architecture and training improvements to bidirectional encoders. For visual document retrieval, ModernVBERT applied a bidirectional ModernBERT-style text encoder while retaining a separate pretrained SigLIP2 vision tower. We wanted to push this even further by designing and training a multimodal encoder without having to carry over the parameter and compute overhead of a VLM.

It has been revealed that neoMME (pronounced "nee-oh-me", IPA /ˈniː.oʊ.mi/) is a multilingual, multimodal foundation encoder that generates vector representations for input text and/or images using a single Transformer encoder. It is not based on an existing pretrained vision tower, text encoder, or text decoder.

Images and text use the same computational path, so NeoMME can more easily support pretraining, fine-tuning, parallelization, and serving across both modalities.

NeoMME comes in two sizes, 260M and 800M. Both variants share the same architecture:.

We pretrain NeoMME from scratch as a discrete masked-diffusion text denoiser. For each text-only example, we sample a corruption rate uniformly between 0 and 1. Each eligible text token is then independently masked at that rate.

Industry observers note that multimodal examples use corruption rates between 0.3 and 1. The image patches remain visible while NeoMME reconstructs masked text. With light masking, the model can often recover a missing word from the surrounding text alone. For example, "cat" is a plausible completion of "The [MASK] sat on the mat," even without an image. But high masking forces the model to learn image-grounded descriptions with little to no signal from the non-masked input text tokens.

It has been revealed that pretraining mixes multilingual text, code, mathematics, natural images, and document images. Each model processes about 524 billion packed input tokens, including 290 billion tokens from text-only examples. This text budget is relatively small compared with ModernBERT's 2 trillion training token budget. Hence, we chose the NorMuon optimizer to improve data efficiency during training.

To get a meaningful downstream evaluation of the backbone, we fine-tune NeoMME for visual document retrieval using the page-image methodology introduced by ColPali. While traditional text-based retrieval consists of retrieving text chunks, NeoMME-Retriever ranks document page screenshots and bypasses all the preprocessing OCR steps necessary to extract text from PDFs. Treating the pages as images preserves layout, charts, tables, font type and size, and other visual clues that cannot be captured even by a perfect OCR model.

NeoMME-Retriever reuses the NeoMME backbone but adds two jointly trained heads on top of it for retrieval:.

Omar Khattab, who introduced late-interaction in ColBERT, explains why the term is more precise than "multi-vector." It describes the granularity and learnability of the scoring function, not simply the number of stored vectors.

To learn more about late-interaction, we recommend reading this crash course by Amélie Chatelain.

In a recent development, one NeoMME-Retriever forward pass returns both representations, which gives you flexibility no matter your use case and infrastructure. We recommend using late-interaction embeddings in general since they are more powerful and can be used easily with open-source libraries like NextPlaid. However, if you have a very large corpora, you can run a single forward pass with NeoMME-Retriever to get the dense embedding, retrieve a small number of documents through an ANN index, and then use late-interaction to rerank the retrieved candidates.

Recent findings suggest that we report nDCG@10 on ViDoRe v3. NeoMME-Retriever-260M reaches 0.523, the highest score among evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters. It is within 0.002 nDCG@10 of ColQwen2.5 while using about 14× fewer parameters. NeoMME-Retriever-800M reaches 0.556, within 0.009 nDCG@10 of the similarly sized Vultron Retriever Flash (0.8B). Both NeoMME-Retriever models lie on the model-size Pareto frontier.

ViDoRe v1 and v2 use nDCG@5. On both benchmarks, NeoMME-Retriever-260M outperforms ColModernVBERT and the twice-larger ColSmol-500M. NeoMME-Retriever-800M outperforms ColPali v1.3 while using 3.6 times fewer parameters.

† Scores from MTEB. ‡ Results from our own evaluations.

Recent findings suggest that late-interaction storage scales linearly with the number of vectors in the output embedding. Higher-resolution images contain more patches, so they produce larger embeddings. For example, a 2048×2048 square page produces embeddings containing 4,200 vectors with NeoMME-Retriever, or about 2.1 MB in float32. Across the ViDoRe v3 benchmark, the measured average is about 1.5 MB per document.

To reduce the storage footprint of the late-interaction index, we combine two complementary compression methods:.

We tested this setup on ViDoRe v3. With a pooling factor 10 and int8 queries and documents, storage decreased from about 1.5 MB to 39 kB per page, a 39× reduction, while keeping more than 99% of the baseline nDCG@10. A more aggressive configuration uses pooling factor 8, int8 queries, and binary documents. That version uses 6 kB per page (255× smaller) and keeps more than 95% of the original retrieval quality.

Users can pick a compression setting from that frontier based on storage budget and required retrieval quality.

Before you can search a corpus, a retriever model must turn your documents into embeddings, which will be stored in a vector store like Qdrant, Weaviate, or Milvus. Faster encoding makes building and adding newly introduced documents to the index faster, thus reducing the GPU uptime and compute cost required.

So we measured image encoding speeds for NeoMME-Retriever against other multimodal document retrievers. We used preprocessed image tensors and calibrated the batch size separately for each model and image size. At a matched 2048×2048 input size on one NVIDIA L40S, NeoMME-Retriever-260M encodes about 51 pages per second, nearly twice ColModernVBERT's 26 pages per second. Both 260M and 800M NeoMME-Retriever models are also faster than the other models we compared on smaller input images.

NeoMME-Retriever (260M and 800M) returns dense and multi-vector embeddings together. The example below scores two text queries against two document-page images with MeanMaxSim late interaction and dense cosine similarity.

It has been revealed that we provide separate dense and late-interaction checkpoints for fine-tuning with Sentence Transformers v6. Following the same pattern as text encoders such as ModernBERT, Sentence Transformers loads the backbone through NeoMMEModel rather than the dual-head NeoMMEForRetrieval class. Sentence Transformers presently supports one retrieval head per model, so each checkpoint lets you fine-tune the dense or late-interaction head independently. To train both heads together, use NeoMMEForRetrieval with a custom Trainer.

Recent findings suggest that visual document retrieval can be used as the first stage of a visual retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system. Unlike text RAG, which retrieves extracted text chunks, visual RAG retrieves the original page images and sends them to a visual language model. The model can then use tables, plots, diagrams, and page layout that text extraction may flatten or omit. Here is how visual RAG works:.

You can test visual RAG directly with NeoMME-Retriever in our HF Space: 🤗 tonywu71/neomme-retriever-demo.

According to recent reports, neoMME replaces separate pretrained image and text encoders with one long-context bidirectional Transformer. We train it from scratch to process both multilingual text tokens and raw 32×32 image patches.

NeoMME-Retriever is a fine-tuned version of NeoMME for visual document retrieval. One forward pass produces both dense and late-interaction representations. The 260M model outperforms all evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters and, at a matched 2048×2048 input size, encodes pages at about 2× ColModernVBERT's throughput. To reduce the large storage footprint of late-interaction embeddings for high-resolution documents, we experimented with hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization and managed to reduce the late-interaction embeddings from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page, a 255× compression, while retaining more than 95% of the baseline nDCG@10.

We release all NeoMME model checkpoints and a day-zero Hugging Face Transformers implementation to allow practitioners to build efficient multimodal and multilingual representation models on top of our work.

NeoMME began as a side quest between two good friends. We worked with limited time and compute, and we decided to share the results so the community can build on them. We thank H Manufacturer for supporting the work and providing the compute used to train NeoMME.

Amazon Connect Customer now lets agents merge and link related cases in the agent workspace, so they can resolve customer concerns faster and respond consistently. When a customer contacts a business about the same problem more than once, or on different channels, the history can end up split across several cases. Agents can merge those cases into one case with a single, consolidated history. For example, an agent can merge the chat and email cases a customer opened about a delayed shipment.

Agents can also link related cases, such as cases from different customers affected by the same glitch, so they can coordinate one consistent response for every affected customer.

Industry observers note that cases is available in the following AWS regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (London), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Africa (Cape Town). To learn more and get started, visit the Cases webpage and documentation.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.22374v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AutoE2E is an open-source end-to-end driving model developed by the Autoware Foundation Robotaxi Working Group. It introduces a temporal bird's-eye-view (BEV) architecture that combines multi-camera perception, HD-map information and route conditioning to predict future vehicle motion. The evaluated model uses a pretrained camera-BEV backbone, temporal feature fusion and a lightweight recurrent trajectory planner. It contains approximately 79.9 million parameters, of which approximately 1.45 million are trainable in the evaluated configuration. The v1.0 release provides model checkpoints, training and evaluation code, and DataModelConsole, a dashboard for visualizing and inspecting model experiments. On the KITScenes validation benchmark, the fine-tuned checkpoint achieves an average displacement error (ADE) of 0.745 m and a final displacement error (FDE) of 2.020 m at a three-second prediction horizon. The paper also reports preliminary real-vehicle research conducted with the Technical University of Munich's EDGAR platform, alongside ongoing collaboration with the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology. AutoE2E v1.0 is an early open research release. Its quantitative evaluation is open-loop, and the model has not yet demonstrated validated closed-loop autonomous driving. The release is intended to provide the autonomous-driving community with an inspectable baseline for further research, experimentation and collaborative development.

Seeing What Still Holds: How Waiting Control Changes Cooperative Recovery

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (196 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.22368v1 Announce Type: latest Abstract: Changing the holding reference during a fixed-duration wait can reverse the ranking of visual recovery methods. We introduce AuditEmbodied, a paired execution and trajectory evaluation framework that independently varies holding references and waiting duration while keeping recovery executors frozen. A 960-execution factorial on 20 initialization seeds compares CAD-feedback and landmark-based recovery from identical post-wait physical states within each holding and waiting condition. Protected completion requires successful recovery under the declared execution constraints. At a 1 s wait with registered wrist references, their protected completion counts change from 6/40 versus 19/40 under registered holding to 34/40 versus 22/40 under position-only holding. Trajectory analysis localizes the main separation to grasp formation: small observation-time target residuals precede large tracking errors. Joint diagnostics and controlled interventions characterize persistent tracking constraints. On fresh seeds, gradual position reanchoring improves CAD recovery's long-wait completion by 42.5 percentage points and reduces mean complete recovery time by 6.06 s relative to registered holding. Additional evaluations with pretrained policies, handover, and a mass-matched geometry characterize holding-reference sensitivity across executors and physical regimes. These findings establish holding reference as an explicit evaluation condition for comparing visual recovery performance.

  • Recent findings suggest that you can open the Airflow UI from the Amazon MWAA console, the AWS CLI, or the API.
  • This feature is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon MWAA Serverless is available.

Amazon MWAA Serverless provides the native Apache Airflow UI for your workflows. You can browse workflows, inspect workflow runs and task instances, read task logs, view a workflow's source and versions, and start a workflow run. The UI uses the permissions of the IAM identity that opens it and reveals only what that identity can read, so read-only access is possible. AWS CloudTrail records the calls the UI makes under your identity.

Recent findings suggest that you can open the Airflow UI from the Amazon MWAA console, the AWS CLI, or the API. Teams already familiar with Airflow can use the interface they know to work with their workflows.

This feature is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon MWAA Serverless is available. For more information, see the AWS Region table.

To get started, see Access the Airflow UI. Apache Airflow is a trademark of the Apache Software Foundation.

#3437. Rebuilding AUTOMATIC1111 with Gradio Workflow

Rebuilding AUTOMATIC1111 with Gradio Workflow

📅 10 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1724 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that in our last post, we built five small gr.Workflow graphs and hinted at what it would take to build something as complex as AUTOMATIC1111's stable-diffusion-webui.
  • Workflow1111 is a graph of eleven media pipelines built using seventy-three nodes.
  • Sources indicate that you can run any of these pipelines by signing in with your Hugging Face account or providing an access token.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in our last post, we built five small gr.Workflow graphs and hinted at what it would take to build something as complex as AUTOMATIC1111's stable-diffusion-webui. In this post we walk you through Workflow1111, where we have rebuilt most of AUTOMATIC1111's feature set as a single workflow canvas.

Workflow1111 is a graph of eleven media pipelines built using seventy-three nodes. It brings together SOTA models for text-to-image, hi-resolution fix, image-to-image, prompt-matrix grids, VLM interrogate, detection-to-inpaint masks, ControlNet-style annotators, background removal, PNG Info storing, and image-to-video.

Sources indicate that you can run any of these pipelines by signing in with your Hugging Face account or providing an access token. Once you sign in, the model calls use your own quota.

👉 Try Workflow1111, or duplicate the Space and start rewiring it for your own use case.

All the media pipelines are built from the same four operator kinds covered in our last post and the official guide. Each node on the canvas wraps one operator, and the operator's inputs and outputs become the ports you connect edges to. As a quick reference on our four operator kinds: fn is a Python function, model is a model called through InferenceClient, space is another Gradio Space, and dataset is a row from a Hub dataset.

Let's go through the pipelines one by one.

This is the core pipeline. It has the controls you'd expect from A1111's txt2img tab: negative prompt, steps, CFG, seed, width and height, plus a model_id field for choosing the checkpoint. The prompt goes through a prompt-builder fn node first, which appends the selected style preset and cleans up the text, then into a model node that calls the checkpoint through Inference Providers. A post-process fn node writes the generation parameters into the PNG's metadata on the way out, which is what the PNG Info pipeline reads back later.

Sources indicate that in Automatic1111, hi-resolution fix first upscales the txt2img output and then runs a second denoising pass. Here it's a two-node detour instead. The text-to-image result goes into a FLUX.1-Kontext model node with a refine instruction ("enhance fine detail and micro-texture, keep the composition identical") and comes back sharper and larger.

That same Kontext node doubles as the image-to-image tab. Upload an image, describe the change you want, and it returns the edited image.

Start with a rough prompt like "A lighthouse in a storm." This pipeline sends it to a Qwen3-4B model node, and a small fn node turns the reply into a clean list of tags, capped at forty: "stormy sea, wet rocks, dramatic composition, low angle shot, volumetric lighting, ominous tone." You can connect any diffusion model node to this output to render the image.

There's no custom node involved, unlike in ComfyUI. In a Gradio workflow the LLM and the diffusion model are both ordinary model operators on the same canvas.

According to recent reports, this is like AUTOMATIC1111's Interrogate button, with a VLM doing the interrogating instead of CLIP. Qwen2.5-VL looks at a night-market photo and writes a prompt that could have produced it. A ViT classifier node reads the same image and returns labels: restaurant 51.9%, tobacco shop 15.6%, toyshop 9.1%.

Both nodes use the same image input, so gr.Workflow runs them in parallel and you get both answers in roughly the time it takes to run one.

Recent findings suggest that AUTOMATIC1111 makes you paint an inpaint mask by hand. This pipeline generates one from a detector instead. DETR finds six objects in a street photo (three people, a dog, a bicycle, and a car), and from there the workflow splits into two branches: one draws the detected boxes on the original image, the other turns them into a mask you can feed into an inpaint pipeline downstream.

Industry observers note that the drawing and the mask creation both happen locally with Pillow and NumPy. Only the detection call leaves the machine.

This is like AUTOMATIC1111's prompt matrix. A base prompt, "a lone oak tree," gets combined with four suffixes (at sunrise, in a thunderstorm, under the Milky Way, in autumn fog) by a fn node, and each variant goes to its own text-to-image node. A final node stitches the four results into one contact sheet.

It has been revealed that gr.Workflow has no loop operator, so the four text-to-image nodes sit side by side on the canvas. Since they're at the same dependency depth they run in parallel, and all four images start generating at once.

Recent findings suggest that this is like the Extras tab in Automatic1111. There are two upscaler nodes, and they take different routes. The first is a local Lanczos resample in an fn node, which needs no network call and finishes as fast as Pillow can resize. The second is AuraSR ×4, and it's the first space node on the canvas: it calls a Space on the Hub and treats the result like any other node output.

Background removal works the same way. BRIA RMBG-2.0 is another space node, so the whole model lives in its own Space and this canvas just calls it in.

Canny, line art, sketch, luma-depth, and posterize are the preprocessors you'd normally get from the ControlNet extension in Automatic1111. Here, each one is a fn node written in plain NumPy, with no model behind it. On a pre-loaded example photo of a building facade, each annotator takes about half a second on CPU.

Recent findings suggest that there are 36 operator nodes in the app, 32 are fn nodes, and 22 of those run entirely in-process without a network call. Roughly two-thirds of the canvas keeps working if you lose your connection. Since these are regular Python functions, you can also test them directly, with no canvas, server, or GPU involved.

It has been revealed that AUTOMATIC1111 stores generation details in the PNG's parameters text chunk, and the PNG Info tab reads them back. Workflow1111 does the same. The post-process node on the text-to-image pipeline writes the metadata, and this pipeline reads it back out, including the prompt, negative prompt, steps, CFG, seed, image size, and model.

Industry observers note that the image node that PNG Info reads from also feeds a Wan 2.2 I2V A14B node, which animates it; in the demo example a sleeping fox wakes up and starts moving. There's no second upload box because one reference node can feed as many downstream pipelines as you need, so a single upload gets its metadata read and gets animated on the same canvas.

So far every model call has gone to someone else's hardware, through Inference Providers or a Space. That's why you can build and run something like Workflow1111 without a GPU of your own.

Sources indicate that A fn node is just Python, though, so it can equally load a model locally and run it on your own GPU. FastVideo/fastvideo-fasth3-preview is a gr.Workflow app that does exactly that. It runs FastH3, a four-step distillation of MiniMax-H3, and generates video with a soundtrack on ZeroGPU.

The whole app comes down to one bound function:.

In a recent development, zeroGPU gives the function a GPU when it needs one, then releases it when the call is done. gr.Workflow doesn't need to know about any of that. It just calls the fn node.

Recent findings suggest that this isn't specific to Spaces either. Point bind= to a function that loads a local checkpoint, run .launch() on your own machine, and the Workflow1111 canvas can drive your own GPU.

Every output node on the canvas becomes a REST endpoint, with no routes written by hand. Workflow1111 exposes nine of them: /image, /edited_image, /generated_prompt, /recovered_prompt, /detected_objects, /x_y_grid, /upscaled_local, /annotator_map, and /png_info.

The same endpoints are also MCP tools. Launch with mcp_server=True (guide) and every output node shows up as a tool an AI assistant can call. Point Claude Code, Cursor, or any MCP client at the server URL:.

In a recent development, now an agent can generate an image, read a prompt back out, or run detection as steps in a larger task, with no glue code. Each caller sends their own token in the X-HF-Token header, so the Space holds none of its own.

AUTOMATIC1111 gave us the feature list, but the tool Gradio Workflow really gets compared to is ComfyUI, since both are node graphs. For a lot of what people want to build and ship, gr.Workflow covers the same ground.

The result is a multi-model pipeline that people can open in a browser, sign into, use right away, and call from code.

Workflow1111 has 73 nodes, but it started with just this:.

It has been revealed that bind= turns your functions into nodes, edges= connects them, and .launch() opens the canvas in your browser so you can keep editing there. When it's ready, gradio deploy puts the whole thing on a Space. The gr.Workflow guide has the full details, including the JSON schema and every operator type.

If you'd rather start from something that already works, open Workflow1111, hit Duplicate, and pick one of the eleven pipelines to change: delete nodes, swap models, rewire the flow. If you'd rather start smaller, the previous post has five workflows you can get running in about a minute each.

Recent findings suggest that whatever you build, post it on X and tag @gradio. We'd be happy to amplify your workflows.

Industry observers note that really impressive breakdown the part that stands out most is how the graph structure gives you free parallelism (the prompt-matrix and interrogate examples) without any extra orchestration code. The mix of fn, model, and space node types on one canvas also makes the ComfyUI comparison land well: you get custom-node flexibility from plain Python, but zero-code REST/MCP endpoints for free. Curious how complex a canvas can get before performance or maintainability becomes a concern has anyone pushed past 73 nodes.

Analisis yang sangat mengesankan, bagian yang paling menonjol adalah bagaimana struktur graf memberikan paralelisme gratis (contoh prompt-matrix dan interrogate) tanpa kode orkestrasi tambahan. Perpaduan tipe node fn, model, dan space pada satu kanvas juga membuat perbandingan dengan ComfyUI tepat: Anda mendapatkan fleksibilitas node kustom dari Python biasa, tetapi endpoint REST/MCP tanpa kode secara gratis. Saya penasaran seberapa kompleks sebuah kanvas dapat dibuat sebelum kinerja atau pemeliharaan menjadi masalah, apakah ada yang pernah melampaui 73 node?

How ISVs are unlocking European workloads using Google Cloud Dedicated technology

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Product Lead, Google Cloud Dedicated.

Product Manager, Google Cloud Dedicated.

The front door to AI in the workplace.

Across Europe, organizations handling sensitive workloads in regulated sectors — such as financial services, healthcare, critical infrastructure, and the public sector — are trying to modernize their infrastructure while adhering to strict local data governance standards, including SecNumCloud in France and BSI C3A in Germany.

According to recent reports, to help organizations accomplish this, Google Cloud Dedicated provides the architectural, security, and API consistency of Google Cloud in locally governed environments managed by independent domestic operators. But infrastructure is only the starting point. Organizations also need to transform the software ecosystem they rely on every day.

According to recent reports, to meet regional sovereignty requirements, organizations acquire and run these software solutions through trusted local entities — such as S3NS in France (a joint venture majority-owned and managed by Thales) and a newly formed German entity that will also be owned and managed by Thales, presently in preview. These local entities operate dedicated infrastructure stacks, help maintain operational custody, and handle customer data within independent jurisdictional boundaries.

Today, we are highlighting the expanding independent software vendor (ISV) ecosystem validated on Google Cloud Dedicated, enabling French and German organizations to run their critical enterprise software in environments designed to support their sovereign and regulatory needs.

Deploying in a sovereign boundary should not require an organization to sacrifice software choice or rewrite its enterprise applications.Because Google Cloud Dedicated provides architectural and API consistency with Google Cloud, validated enterprise software runs directly inside these partner-operated environments without custom re-platforming.

This model provides European enterprises with three concrete advantages:.

Localized operational custody: Infrastructure operations, software quarantine procedures, and day-to-day administrative access are under the direct management of local European partners operating with specialized remote technical escalations governed by strict, partner-supervised escorted access controls.

Broad software choice: Regulated institutions can deploy industry-standard tools for identity governance, cyber resilience, simulation, and data streaming natively in their sovereign perimeter.

Streamlined compliance: Organizations fulfill national frameworks like SecNumCloud and BSI guidelines while preserving familiar CI/CD pipelines, APIs, and developer workflows.

When highly regulated European institutions consider moving to a sovereign cloud, the infrastructure itself is rarely the primary roadblock. The real bottleneck is software.Historically, pursuing strict sovereignty meant accepting compromises:.

Rewriting applications from scratch or maintaining custom, brittle tooling because mainstream enterprise platforms were unavailable.

Forcing security, engineering, and data teams to abandon the industry-standard tools they use daily in favor of untested niche alternatives.

Sidelining high-impact initiatives like real-time fraud scoring, automated DevSecOps, and modern identity governance simply because the required ISVs could not legally or technically operate in the environment.

Because Google Cloud Dedicated maintains architectural and API consistency with Google Cloud, leading global and European software providers can deploy their proven platforms directly inside national, domestic operator-managed boundaries. Regulated organizations retain the software, automated pipelines, and operational standards they rely on — without sacrificing compliance or operational custody.

Deploying enterprise software on Google Cloud Dedicated and S3NS isn't just about hosting an application locally; it’s about pairing proven software engines with sovereign operations. Here is how these joint architectures unlock strategic value for European enterprises:.

In a recent development, cohesity on Google Cloud Dedicated (Sovereign cyber resilience): Cohesity has many options to meet organizational data sovereignty objectives, whether on-premises or in the cloud with Google Cloud Dedicated. This is done through a unified, cyber resilient, AI-powered data platform — Cohesity Data Cloud — that is sovereign-by-design, making it easier to protect, manage, recover, and have visibility into data, while supporting compliance with data sovereignty requirements. For example, running Cohesity directly in the S3NS perimeter combines Cohesity’s Zero Trust cyber resilience architecture designed for immutability with local operational custody. Customers gain advanced threat hunting, cyber vaulting, and recovery orchestration that powers quick, clean, and trusted cyber-recovery from ransomware threats without allowing diagnostic telemetry, secondary backup copies, or operational keys to traverse external networks.

GitLab on Google Cloud Dedicated (Secure, compliant software delivery pipelines): Combining GitLab’s DevSecOps platform with Google Cloud Dedicated allows defense, aerospace, and public sector engineering teams to ship code at commercial velocity. Proprietary source code, vulnerability scans, and CI/CD artifact registries stay contained behind the partner-operated boundary, significantly reducing audit friction of using public SaaS code repositories.

Recent findings suggest that ansys, part of Synopsys, on Google Cloud Dedicated (High-performance sovereign engineering simulation): Pairing Ansys, part of Synopsys, high-performance computing simulation workflows with the dedicated compute clusters of Google Cloud Dedicated gives European manufacturers the massive scale needed for aerodynamic, fluid, and structural modeling. Highly sensitive intellectual property, blueprints, and digital twins designed to keep intellectual property within regional boundaries and national jurisdiction while running at cloud speed.

Recent findings suggest that memority on Google Cloud Dedicated / S3NS (Audit-ready sovereign identity governance): Integrating Memority’s identity factory platform directly into the S3NS SecNumCloud-qualified environment provides regulated entities with capabilities designed to support their NIS2 and DORA compliance requirements with the PREMI3NS SecNumCloud-qualified environment. Organizations can manage and audit millions of identities without building custom IAM infrastructure or exposing access tokens to non-European cloud services."Our customers — from critical infrastructure operators to financial institutions — share the same requirement: an enterprise-grade IAM platform capable of managing millions of identities while meeting the highest standards of digital sovereignty. As NIS2 and DORA reshape the regulatory landscape, this requirement has become a business-critical imperative. S3NS enables us to address it at scale by providing a comprehensive IAM platform hosted in a SecNumCloud-qualified cloud environment, with built-in capabilities supporting the auditability, traceability, and operational resilience expected under these regulations,” said Francis Grégoire, Deputy CEO, Memority.

In a recent development, rackWare on Google Cloud Dedicated (De-risked cloud migration): Running RackWare’s automated migration and disaster recovery engines on Google Cloud Dedicated gives organizations a low-friction bridge from on-premises data centers into sovereign cloud environments. Teams can replicate, synchronize, and failover complex enterprise operating environments, bypassing the prohibitive cost and timeline of manual application refactoring.

According to recent reports, striim on Google Cloud Dedicated (Real-time data streaming without jurisdictional risk): Combining Striim’s continuous change data capture engine with the local boundaries of Google Cloud Dedicated enables organizations to feed live operational analytics and fraud models without batch delays. Financial institutions and logistics leaders can stream sensitive customer and payment transactions in sub-second intervals, with strong technical assurances that streaming pipelines remain bound to local infrastructure."Regulated organizations should not have to choose between modern, real-time data and the control their environments demand. By making Striim available on Google Cloud Dedicated, we can help customers securely move and continuously deliver trusted data to the systems that power critical operations, analytics, and AI without ever compromising on sovereignty or resilience,” said Phillip Cockrell, SVP of Business Development, Striim.UPS Capital integrated Striim’s real-time streaming technology with analytics models to power its DeliveryDefense address verification and delivery security system. By streaming and validating transaction and delivery data continuously without batch lag, UPS assesses risk scoring in real time — a capability European logistics and financial operators can now deploy directly in their sovereign boundary.

Industry observers note that red Hat on Google Cloud Dedicated (Operational consistency on open hybrid platforms): Deploying Red Hat Enterprise Linux and OpenShift across Google Cloud Dedicated bridges on-premises infrastructure and sovereign cloud environments. Engineering teams maintain their existing operating runtimes, container standards, and administrative toolsets across sites, avoiding vendor lock-in and eliminating the operational retraining typically required when moving to sovereign stacks.

In a recent development, saviynt on Google Cloud Dedicated (Zero-trust access governance across sovereign assets): Deploying Saviynt’s privileged access management and identity governance inside the sovereign boundary allows enterprises to centrally enforce least-privilege security across critical databases and workloads. Security administrators maintain automated role lifecycles and complete audit logs without exposing access intelligence to offshore management planes.

Tsuga on Google Cloud Dedicated (Telemetry and observability): Tsuga’s bring-your-own-cloud (BYOC) observability platform deployed inside a customer's dedicated VPC resolves one of the biggest security exposures in regulated IT: transmitting production telemetry to third-party SaaS monitoring providers. By processing all traces, metrics, and logs on local storage, organizations achieve full observability, reduce external data egress costs, and help protect sensitive operational data.

MongoDB on Google Cloud Dedicated (Modern data velocity with domestic residency): Running MongoDB Enterprise Advanced on Google Cloud Dedicated gives developers the flexibility of the document model while adhering to strict regional isolation requirements. Regulated organizations can rapidly build modern, real-time applications and customer portals using modern development patterns without being forced onto legacy relational database architectures.

It has been revealed that ispirer on Google Cloud Dedicated (Automated legacy modernization): Pairing Ispirer’s automated database conversion toolkit with Google Cloud Dedicated addresses a key friction point in database modernization: the complexity of migrating legacy database engines. Automated code and schema conversion shrinks complex multi-year migration timelines into predictable, low-risk deployments on modern sovereign infrastructure."Every migration is really a risk decision. Offering the Ispirer toolkit on Google Cloud Dedicated gives customers over 27 years of deterministic conversion experience—that's the value we consistently hear back from client teams,” remarked Natallia Bespalova, CEO, Ispirer Systems.

Recent findings suggest that splunk integration with Google Cloud Dedicated (sovereign log collection, observability, and SIEM integration): Splunk now supports Google Cloud Dedicated as a first-class log source. Extensions to the open-source OpenTelemetry Collector allow organizations to export logs from Google Cloud Dedicated environments into Splunk Enterprise using the Google Cloud Pub/Sub receiver and the Splunk HTTP Event Collector (HEC) exporter, alongside enhancements to the Splunk Add-on for Google Cloud for direct log collection Additionally, Splunk Observability Cloud now supports Google Cloud Dedicated through its Infrastructure Monitoring cloud integration, which connects projects to pull metrics and metadata from services so teams can monitor resource and application health. Critical infrastructure and financial institutions can now centralize security analytics, performance monitoring, SIEM operations, and incident response while keeping audit logs, threat intelligence, and sensitive operational telemetry within national boundaries.

Industry observers note that solo.io on Google Cloud Dedicated (Kubernetes-native governance and runtime for AI agents): kagent from Solo.io adds a Kubernetes-native runtime for AI agents and their MCP tool servers on Google Cloud Dedicated, declared and governed through the same GitOps and RBAC workflows platform teams already operate. Lifecycle control, agent-level access policy, and human-in-the-loop approval are built in, helping organizations ensure agents are deployed, audited, and managed within the local partner perimeter.

Pelico on Google Cloud Dedicated (Sovereign supply chain resilience for aerospace and defense): Running Pelico on Google Cloud Dedicated with S3NS PREMI3NS gives industrial manufacturers the ability to turn ERP and planning data into clear operational priorities while keeping sensitive data under European sovereign control. Proven for a global aerospace and defense group, this architecture lets sovereignty-minded organizations anticipate and resolve supply chain disruptions using the capabilities of Pelico’s cloud offering, without compromising strict regional isolation or domestic operational custody.

We evaluate health context learning: acquiring, integrating, and applying relevant context during inference with fixed model parameters to answer health questions and respond appropriately to changes in facts, evidence, or task goals. 💡 Key Takeaways

  • With IAM Identity Center integration, owners sign in to the Apache Airflow UI with their corporate identity provider.
  • In a recent development, with multi-team environments, several teams can share a single MWAA environment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow (Amazon MWAA) now supports fine-grained access control, giving administrators precise control over who can access which workflows and resources in an Apache Airflow environment. Fine-grained access control is delivered through two upcoming capabilities: IAM Identity Center integration and multi-team environments.

With IAM Identity Center integration, owners sign in to the Apache Airflow UI with their corporate identity provider. Authorization is evaluated per request using IAM policies attached to IAM Identity Center Permission Sets, with condition keys that scope access by resource type (DAGs, connections, variables, pools, and more), action, and specific resource ID.

In a recent development, with multi-team environments, several teams can share a single MWAA environment. Each team gets its own DAG folder in Amazon S3, and owners see only shared DAGs plus their own teams' DAGs based on IAM Identity Center group membership. Teams reduce cost through shared infrastructure and simplify management by configuring environment settings once. Multi-team environments are based on the Apache Airflow multi-team feature, which is currently in preview.

These features are available in all AWS Regions where Amazon MWAA is available.

To learn more, visit the IAM Identity Center integration documentation and the multi-team environments documentation.
