Industry News: Sovereign AI in Europe: Fresh ways to control your AI stack

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1143 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, today in Brussels, public sector leaders, policymakers and partners are meeting at the Sovereign AI Summit to discuss how to build the next decade of Europe's public services, healthcare, and finance with AI under European control.
  • Achieving that goal takes more than deciding where data is stored.
  • Will choosing more control mean settling for less capable AI?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

VP & GM, Regulated & Sovereign Cloud.

The front door to AI in the workplace.

In a recent development, today in Brussels, public sector leaders, policymakers and partners are meeting at the Sovereign AI Summit to discuss how to build the next decade of Europe's public services, healthcare, and finance with AI under European control. We're here with our European partners to help deliver it.

Achieving that goal takes more than deciding where data is stored. When we talk with European organizations, we hear four common questions from them:.

Will choosing more control mean settling for less capable AI?

Who can access our data, and can we prove to regulators that our controls work?

Will the value that organizations create with AI stay in Europe?

How can we keep AI running reliably?

Sources indicate that in May 2025, we introduced a portfolio of sovereign cloud offerings for customers to match their desired level of control to each workload. In February, we set out the commitments behind that portfolio, covering local investment, operational continuity, customer control over data, and open technology.

Today, we’re building on these commitments. Gemini models are coming to Google Cloud Dedicated, our partner-operated cloud, expanding model choice beyond the open models already available in the model garden. We are also announcing new capabilities for cryptographic key control and compliance, and new work with European software companies and startups.

According to recent reports, sovereignty is not one-size-fits-all, so Sovereign Cloud from Google offers three ways to run a workload. First, Google Cloud Data Boundary applies data residency, access, and encryption controls on our public cloud. A second option is Google Cloud Dedicated, which is operated by an independent local partner on isolated infrastructure. And finally, Google Distributed Cloud runs in a customer's own data center connected or fully air-gapped.

Recent findings suggest that select Gemini models are already available in Google Cloud with a commitment to perform machine-learning processing of customer data in-region for these models, including within the EU. It is also available with Google Distributed Cloud. And with today’s announcement that Gemini is coming to Google Cloud Dedicated, organizations that require a locally operated cloud will be able to use it there too.

It has been revealed that many teams also want open models, or models they have tuned themselves. In France, S3NS has made managed model serving and inference generally available on PREMI3NS, its cloud built on Google Cloud Dedicated. Teams can deploy open models from providers such as Mistral and Google through Model Garden, or bring their own models. S3NS operates the environment, designed so the deployed models and prompts remain within the PREMI3NS environment under S3NS's control.

Industry observers note that for many European organizations, data access, encryption key access and services access dictate their sovereignty posture. On our public cloud, customers can already see when Google personnel access their data and why, approve or deny that access with Access Transparency, Access Approval, and Key Access Justifications. Customers who want  more control can hold their encryption keys outside Google Cloud, which enables them to deny access to their data for any reason. Together, these controls help ensure the customer controls any and all access to their data.

Recent findings suggest that when customers hold keys outside Google Cloud, every key request has to travel to an external system, which can add latency and availability risk. Confidential External Key Management (cEKM), right now in preview, is designed to remove that trade-off: Customers, or their chosen local partner, hold and control access to the root keys outside Google Cloud, while key operations run inside a hardware-attested Confidential Computing environment designed to run with the low latency and reliability that data-intensive workloads, including AI, demand.

Customers can also ask trusted local partners to hold their keys external from Google infrastructure. A fresh partnership with Telefónica in Spain (currently in preview) expands customer options beyond existing European partnerships France, Germany, Italy, Spain.

In a recent development, auditing sovereignty controls and requirements is not only difficult, it often requires engineering effort. To help make audits smoother, we are introducing Data Boundary frameworks that map local and regional regulatory requirements to enforced, auditable controls. A framework for Switzerland is available today, and a framework for the EU's Digital Operational Resilience (DORA) Act is planned for financial services organizations.

With Audit Manager, customers can start from a ready-made framework, adapt it to their own policies, and give auditors continuous, machine-readable evidence, designed to keep customer data within their designated boundary.

According to recent reports, sovereignty also depends on who operates the technology, and whether the value it creates stays local. That's why we work with European companies at every layer: those that operate the cloud, those that build software for it, and the startups that will build what comes next.

Google Cloud Dedicated is designed so that the local partner controls the environment, can block software updates in exceptional circumstances, and can keep operating for up to 12 months in the unlikely scenario that its Dedicated instance connection to Google is severed. These design choices sit alongside the commitments we made in February, including that should Google receive an order from a national government to suspend or terminate the provision of Google Cloud's operations provided from any country, we will seek to limit, modify, or object to any such order using all available legal avenues.

In France, PREMI3NS from S3NS has achieved SecNumCloud 3.2 qualification from ANSSI, France's national cybersecurity agency. With Thales, we are extending Google Cloud Dedicated to Germany (currently in preview), to enable a sovereign hyperscale capability across the EU.

Regulated workloads often stall because the security, identity, and monitoring tools that teams depend on are not available in a sovereign environment. More than a dozen software vendors have now validated their products on Google Cloud Dedicated, including European providers such as Memority and Tsuga.

We also want to help the newly introduced companies and skills that AI is creating  to take root in Europe. The new Google for Startups Accelerator: Sovereign AI is an equity-free program that gives startups in regulated sectors support from Google engineers, mentorship, and access to local cloud providers.

We are continuing to build on the strategy we set in 2025: giving customers control that they can verify, a choice in  how they operate in the cloud and who operates the environment, and access to advanced AI regardless of your deployment choices. We will keep bringing more of our AI platform to partner-operated and on-premises environments, extending access and key controls to more services, and adding frameworks for more regulations, together with the European partners who operate these services.

To learn more, visit Sovereign Cloud from Google or talk to a sovereign specialist.

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (251 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

ConfGuard: a physics-grounded reference monitor for predictive-maintenance large-language-model agents

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (251 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.22288v1 Announce Type: fresh Abstract: Large-language-model agents now close the industrial predictive-maintenance loop, reading sensor windows, retrieving procedures and dispatching work orders. Two attack channels meet there: injected text in a retrieved document can hijack the decision, and a bounded sensor perturbation can corrupt the remaining-useful-life estimate behind it. Recent agent defenses police data provenance and tool privilege but cannot tell whether a prognostic quantity is physically plausible. ConfGuard is a reference monitor with a physics-grounded policy. Its conformal monitor tests each prediction, anchored to the asset's admitted history, against degradation physics: capped remaining life never rises and falls at most one cycle per cycle. Calibrating its threshold over whole asset trajectories lets the operator set the expected share of a clean asset's windows the running monitor escalates. A physics-policy validator checks the agent's maintenance-urgency decision against the decision a deterministic policy derives from the same interval. On all 10,196 C-MAPSS test windows the monitor cuts a covert attacker's reach on healthy assets from 0.529 to 0.046 and closes suppression of failing assets (0.151 to 0), escalating 0.027 of clean windows against a 0.05 target, while the fixed physical range it replaces leaves both attacks open. Behind a Qwen3-14B planner the composed monitors hold urgency-class injection to 0.00 and the universal sensor attack to 0.12, against 0.29 and 0.54 for a defended prompt. An adaptive attacker defeats a Mahalanobis detector on 0.504 of windows and adversarial training on 0.485. We report an attack class the projection misses.

  • The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.
  • AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema.
  • According to recent reports, as AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly important sources of evidence about model and system performance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.

AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema. This next phase of the collaboration puts that shared infrastructure into practice.

According to recent reports, as AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly important sources of evidence about model and system performance. Yet results are reported across many formats, platforms, and outlets, often without enough information to reproduce them. Running the evaluations again may itself be prohibitively expensive.

EvalEval's mission is to improve this ecosystem through a shared reporting schema, Every Eval Ever, and an open platform, Evaluation Cards, that brings evaluation results and the information needed to interpret them into a common structure.

This builds naturally on AISI's work to make evaluation more efficient through OptStop, more statistically rigorous through HiBayES, and more standardised in areas including transcript analysis and capability elicitation. Together, AISI and EvalEval are working to diagnose gaps in evaluation reporting and build shared infrastructure to close them.

Transcript-level transparency matters not only for reproducibility, but also for analysis and diagnosis. In this newly introduced phase of the collaboration, AISI is making publicly reported evaluation methods and findings available through Evaluation Cards where appropriate. The release includes verified results, context, and configuration information for the five benchmarks in the paper's main experiment:.

These results cover six frontier models: Claude Opus 4, Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5, GPT-5.2, and GPT-5.4. The release also includes results from two related cyber evaluations—Cyber CTFs and The Last Ones—which use a different, partially overlapping set of models. The data accompany AISI's paper, How Inference Compute Shapes Frontier LLM Evaluation, which studies how benchmark performance depends on inference-time compute and evaluation protocol.

Performance on Humanity's Last Exam changes with evaluation protocol and inference compute. Each curve indicates the cumulative share of attempted tasks solved within a given token count, using the earliest observed success per task. When models received correctness feedback from an oracle after each attempt, they continued to solve additional tasks as token use increased.

When results are openly released with setup information, researchers and practitioners can examine individual studies more closely and compare findings across the wider ecosystem. Where other reports lack these details, releases like AISI's provide verified reference points for interpreting evaluations in context—for example, by helping researchers understand how setup choices may influence reported performance. As more evaluators adopt EEE, open comparisons like these can support broader and more reliable meta-research.

AISI's Terminal-Bench 2.0 results alongside other reported evaluations for the same models, under different evaluation setups.

We are excited about this adoption and look forward to further standardising and sharing evaluations with AISI and other AI evaluation organisations.

In a recent development, the EvalEval Coalition is a research community developing scientifically grounded research and robust deployment infrastructure for the evaluation ecosystem. Its goal is to improve evaluation science, address the lack of consensus around documenting evaluation applicability and utility, and broaden coverage of the impacts that matter for scientific research and policy analysis.

The coalition's flagship projects include Every Eval Ever, a shared schema and repository for evaluation results, and Evaluation Cards, which combines benchmark metadata, evaluation-run data, and model metadata into interpretable records. Together, they make it easier to understand when apparently similar scores were produced under meaningfully different conditions.

It has been revealed that the UK AI Security Institute is a research organisation within the UK government's Department for Science, Innovation and Technology. Its mission is to equip governments with a scientific understanding of the risks posed by advanced AI. AISI conducts research and builds infrastructure to understand advanced AI capabilities and impacts, develop and test mitigations, and inform policy.

The line that matters for practitioners is quiet: apparently similar scores can be produced under meaningfully different conditions.

Recent findings suggest that once you've watched a benchmark move just by changing inference-time compute or the elicitation protocol, "Model A beat Model B on X" without a card is marketing, not comparison. Evaluation Cards that ship verified results with configuration — especially transcript-level context where it's appropriate — are how eval becomes a contract instead of a leaderboard screenshot.

One ask I'd put to teams adopting EEE: which fields get skipped first under deadline pressure (seed, tool access, attempt budget, oracle feedback), and do you treat a missing field as "do not cite the delta" rather than "assume defaults"?

Sources indicate that reproducible reporting won't remove disagreement. It will make the disagreement about the right variables.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, AWS Marketplace sellers can now submit Value Added Tax (VAT) credit notes for refunded deemed supply transactions through a self-service experience in AWS Partner Central.
  • According to recent reports, sellers can view eligible refund line items in the VAT on deemed supply section, select the refunds covered by a credit note, upload a PDF or the applicable electronic invoice format, and track the submission status.
  • These capabilities are available for eligible AWS Marketplace transactions, including Channel Partner Private Offer (CPPO) transactions, in supported EU member states, Norway, and the United Kingdom.

According to recent reports, AWS Marketplace sellers can now submit Value Added Tax (VAT) credit notes for refunded deemed supply transactions through a self-service experience in AWS Partner Central. Previously, VAT was disbursed to sellers for eligible transactions, and when a buyer was later refunded, sellers had to contact AWS to submit the corresponding credit note. This launch simplifies post-refund VAT documentation for sellers.

According to recent reports, sellers can view eligible refund line items in the VAT on deemed supply section, select the refunds covered by a credit note, upload a PDF or the applicable electronic invoice format, and track the submission status. Sellers can consolidate multiple eligible refunds into a single credit note where applicable and review the associated financial adjustment in the Seller Insights reporting.

These capabilities are available for eligible AWS Marketplace transactions, including Channel Partner Private Offer (CPPO) transactions, in supported EU member states, Norway, and the United Kingdom. Country-specific invoicing and electronic-invoicing requirements continue to apply.

To get started, sign in to AWS Partner Central and go to Settings → Tax information → VAT on deemed supply. To learn more, visit the AWS Marketplace Seller Guide or Deemed Supply FAQs.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Roadzen, which applies AI to insurance and mobility, has secured roughly $10m (₹94 crore) for its Indian subsidiary, Roadzen AI Limited, which is now valued at about $300m post-money on a stand-alone basis.

The round is being raised entirely as common equity. It carries no warrants or preferred rights, and the latest shares rank equally with those held by the existing shareholder, Roadzen. Because the capital goes into the subsidiary, shareholders in the Nasdaq-listed parent will not be diluted. Family offices and capital markets investors anchored the deal. Several of them had backed the company’s earlier India subsidiary round and raised their commitments this time.

As part of the deal, Roadzen is bringing its worldwide operating businesses together under Roadzen AI Limited, which was previously called Roadzen Technologies Limited. Roadzen Inc. will remain the Nasdaq-listed parent and will keep about 89% of the subsidiary.

The money will go towards the group’s fastest-growing priorities in insurance and mobility. It will also shore up the balance sheet and support the company’s aim of reaching an annual revenue run-rate of $100m this fiscal year.

It has been revealed that in the US, Roadzen plans to add sales capacity to pursue several growth opportunities expected in the near term. In India, its AI-powered claims-to-repair business VehicleCare is expected to increase revenue more than tenfold this year. DrivebuddyAI, which Roadzen describes as the only AIS-184-validated driver-safety platform in the country, is expanding as new safety rules take effect.

According to recent reports, roadzen operates at the intersection of insurance and mobility and uses AI across its products. Its platform helps insurers, automakers, and fleets better predict and prevent risk, automate claims, and improve insurance experiences.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Corma, an AI research lab building foundation models for defensive cybersecurity, has secured $125m in Series A funding at a $1bn valuation, only three months after revealing its seed round.
  • Recent findings suggest that NEA led the investment, with participation from returning backers Sequoia Capital, Khosla Ventures and Coatue.
  • Corma’s $60m seed round, led by Sequoia, was declared in August.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Corma, an AI research lab building foundation models for defensive cybersecurity, has secured $125m in Series A funding at a $1bn valuation, only three months after revealing its seed round.

Recent findings suggest that NEA led the investment, with participation from returning backers Sequoia Capital, Khosla Ventures and Coatue. The latest raise takes the company’s total funding to $185m.

Corma’s $60m seed round, led by Sequoia, was declared in August.

The funding arrives as large organisations move promptly to integrate Corma’s model into their security operations amid mounting concern over AI-driven attacks. Since the organization debuted publicly, interest has climbed among Fortune 100, Fortune 500 and Fortune Global 500 businesses, which are handing a growing share of their security workload to Corma’s autonomous AI workforce. To keep pace, the firm has expanded its server capacity 24-fold.

At its August launch, Corma cautioned that AI was advancing far faster on the offensive side than the defensive one. That concern was borne out in October, when a series of serious vulnerabilities and breaches affecting widely used software, nicknamed “Black October,” left security teams under pressure and prompted warnings from governments in Washington, Tokyo and elsewhere.

According to Corma, the imbalance stems from the industry’s focus on coding. As leading labs pour resources into models that write software, those same models become more adept at spotting flaws, since vulnerabilities are effectively bugs. When combined with agents, they can now carry out exploits from start to finish. Defensive work outside code security, however, calls for different skills, such as sifting through large amounts of audit logs, security events and network flows, linking faint signals across systems over extended periods, and remaining consistent through long chains of decisions. Coding models were not designed for these tasks.

Corma trains foundation models specifically for this defensive work and deploys them as an AI workforce that sits alongside human security teams, operating within their existing tools and handling a broad range of security tasks.

Corma co-founder and CEO Alon Pluda mentioned, “Cybersecurity is now a battle of intelligence against intelligence, and Black October made that impossible to ignore. Since we came out of stealth, demand from the world’s largest organizations has been overwhelming, and one of our hardest problems has been securing capacity fast enough to keep up with the demand.

NEA partner Aaron Jacobson remarked, “Corma is building the intelligence layer that defensive security needs. As AI gives attackers an advantage, Corma’s combination of frontier AI research and deep cybersecurity expertise has the potential to help organizations defend against these threats at scale. Corma is the only manufacturer taking this on in a way that is scalable across organizations to prevent the next major cyberattack.”.

Learning Regions of Attraction for Transverse Feedback Linearization under Controller Singularities

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (213 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.22286v1 Announce Type: upcoming Abstract: Transverse feedback linearization (TFL) achieves path following by exactly linearizing the error dynamics, but its controller is undefined on a singular set, such as zero speed for a unicycle or zero thrust for a quadrotor. The constrained region of attraction, the set of initial states from which the closed loop converges to the path without violating state or regularity constraints, determines where the controller can be safely activated. Exploiting the exact linear error dynamics, we show that this region is the largest forward invariant subset of the admissible set. We then decompose its state-constrained Zubov value function into an analytically known quadratic cost-to-go and a safety value function. We learn only the latter, by fitted value iteration without infinite-horizon trajectory labels. The resulting estimate combines an inner layer verified by interval branch and bound with a learned outer layer tested on samples. On a unicycle following a circle and a sinusoid and on a planar quadrotor, it covers on average 72.0%, 83.4% and 19.1% of the simulated region of attraction. In comparison, the quadratic cost-to-go and two physics-informed neural network (PINN) solvers of Zubov's equation cover at most 11.3%, 4.0% and 0.0% on average. Code and animations are available at https://gradslab.github.io/roa_tfl.

Sources indicate that AWS Batch now supports additional Kubernetes security context settings in Amazon EKS job definitions, including Linux capabilities, seccomp profiles, and pod-level settings. For EKS clusters that enforce the Kubernetes Pod Security Standards restricted profile, you can now run AWS Batch jobs with only the privileges and system calls they require.

Recent findings suggest that to get started, use the RegisterJobDefinition API to set capabilities and seccompProfile in a container's securityContext, or set securityContext in podProperties to define pod-wide settings such as fsGroup. Container-level settings override pod-level defaults. You can configure these settings through the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, or AWS CloudFormation.

In a recent development, the additional security context settings for AWS Batch on Amazon EKS are now supported in all AWS Regions where AWS Batch is available. For more information, see the Amazon EKS properties section in the AWS Batch User Guide.
